blocks.text: Two patients are both infected with intracellular organisms. In one, macrophages that ought to kill ingested bacteria fail because a signalling cytokine is missing; in the other, a virus spreads because infected cells are not being destroyed. The first problem is a failure of helper T cell help, the second of cytotoxic killing. Naive T cells are only the starting point; what they become decides what the immune system can do.

blocks.markdown: After a naive T cell is activated in a lymph node, it divides and **differentiates** into effector cells. Which type depends on the cytokines present (signal 3) and the T cell's MHC restriction: **CD4⁺ helper T cells** (restricted by MHC class II) direct other immune cells, **CD8⁺ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs)** (restricted by MHC class I) kill infected or abnormal cells, and **regulatory T cells** restrain the response. A subset of activated cells persists afterwards as **memory T cells**.
**Helper subsets.** Each is defined by the cytokines that drive it, a master transcription factor, the cytokines it secretes and the pathogens it fights:

rows: Activate macrophages to kill intracellular pathogens such as mycobacteria; help CD8⁺ T cells; promote opsonising IgG
Helminths: IgE class switching, eosinophil activation, mucus; implicated in allergic disease
Recruit neutrophils; defence of mucosal surfaces against extracellular bacteria and fungi; implicated in autoimmunity
blocks.caption: Major CD4⁺ helper subsets

blocks.title: Use the cytokine to remember the role
blocks.text: IFN-γ activates macrophages (Th1); IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13 drive IgE and eosinophils (Th2); IL-17 recruits neutrophils (Th17). A related subset, T follicular helper (Tfh) cells, help B cells in germinal centres and are not covered further here.

blocks.title: Which T cell is at work?
blocks.prompt: A mycobacterium is surviving inside the phagosomes of macrophages in a granuloma. Name the helper subset that should help, the cytokines involved and the mechanism by which the macrophage kills.

steps.text: Identify the pathogen type. Mycobacteria live inside macrophages, an intracellular niche.
Choose the subset. Th1 cells are driven by IL-12 from dendritic cells and macrophages and secrete IFN-γ.
Describe the effect. IFN-γ binds its receptor on the macrophage, activating it to increase phagosome-lysosome fusion and microbicidal mechanisms, including reactive oxygen and nitrogen species.
Note the feedback. TNF, also made by Th1 cells, helps maintain the granuloma.

blocks.answer: Th1 cells, via IL-12-driven differentiation and IFN-γ activation of the macrophage.

blocks.markdown: **Cytotoxic T cells.** A CTL recognises viral or tumour peptide on MHC class I through its TCR and CD8. After forming a tight contact (the immunological synapse), it delivers a 'lethal hit' by two main routes. In the **granule pathway**, **perforin** forms pores in the target membrane and **granzymes** (serine proteases such as granzyme B) enter and activate caspases, driving **apoptosis**. In the **Fas pathway**, **Fas ligand** on the CTL binds **Fas (CD95)** on the target, activating caspases through death-domain signalling. Apoptosis is a controlled form of death that limits spillage of virus. The CTL detaches unharmed and can kill again, and also secretes IFN-γ and TNF.

blocks.caption: Killing in a classical release assay: target cells are labelled, mixed with CTLs, and released label is counted

blocks.title: Reading a killing assay
blocks.prompt: Target cells labelled with a radioactive marker are mixed with CTLs. The released counts are: experimental 3,000 counts per minute (cpm); spontaneous (targets alone) 500 cpm; maximum (detergent-lysed) 5,500 cpm. Calculate specific lysis.

steps.text: Subtract spontaneous release from the experimental release.
Subtract spontaneous release from the maximum release.
Divide and convert to a percentage.
The spontaneous release is subtracted because some label leaks from healthy cells; without correction killing would be overestimated.

blocks.markdown: **Regulatory T cells (Tregs).** Tregs are CD4⁺ cells that express the high-affinity IL-2 receptor chain **CD25** and the transcription factor **FOXP3**. They suppress other T cells by secreting inhibitory cytokines (IL-10, TGF-β), by consuming IL-2 (depriving effector cells of a growth factor), and via CTLA-4 on their surface, which removes CD80/CD86 from antigen-presenting cells. By limiting the intensity and duration of responses, they prevent tissue damage and autoimmunity. Loss-of-function mutations in FOXP3 cause **IPEX** (immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, enteropathy, X-linked syndrome), with severe early autoimmunity.

rows: Perforin/granzyme and Fas-mediated killing of target
Suppression via IL-10, TGF-β, IL-2 consumption, CTLA-4

points: Helper subsets are Th1 (IL-12, IFN-γ, macrophage activation), Th2 (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13: IgE, eosinophils, helminths) and Th17 (IL-17: neutrophils, mucosal defence).
CTLs recognise peptide on MHC class I and kill by perforin and granzymes (apoptosis) or Fas ligand.
Tregs (CD4, CD25, FOXP3) limit immune responses with IL-10, TGF-β and IL-2 consumption; FOXP3 loss causes IPEX.

questions.stem: Which cytokine is the signature product of Th1 cells and activates macrophages?

distractorRationale.b: IL-5 is a Th2 cytokine and recruits eosinophils.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: IFN-γ activates macrophages for killing of intracellular pathogens.
distractorRationale.d: IL-17 is the Th17 cytokine recruiting neutrophils.

questions.explanation: Th1 cells secrete IFN-γ, which activates macrophages to destroy ingested microbes. IL-4/IL-5 belong to Th2, IL-17 to Th17.

questions.stem: A child has chronic mucosal Candida infections and recurrent skin staphylococcal abscesses with low circulating IL-17 activity. Which helper subset is functionally deficient?

distractorRationale.a: Th1 deficiency causes susceptibility to intracellular organisms such as mycobacteria.
distractorRationale.b: Th2 deficiency would affect helminth and IgE responses.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: Th17 cells recruit neutrophils and defend mucosa against fungi and extracellular bacteria.

questions.explanation: IL-17 and IL-22 from Th17 cells promote neutrophil recruitment and epithelial antimicrobial defence, particularly against Candida and Staphylococcus. Its loss produces this pattern.

questions.stem: Which subset and cytokines are most relevant to defence against a helminth worm?

options.text: Th2 with IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13

questions.correctOptionText: Th2 with IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13

distractorRationale.b: Correct: IL-4 drives IgE, IL-5 eosinophils and IL-13 mucus and smooth muscle responses.
distractorRationale.c: Th17 mainly handles extracellular bacteria and fungi.
distractorRationale.d: CTLs kill infected cells, not large extracellular parasites.

questions.explanation: Th2 cytokines drive the eosinophil and IgE response that expels helminths. This same pathway is overactive in allergy.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly describes the granule pathway of CTL killing?

options.text: Perforin forms pores; granzymes induce apoptosis
Fas ligand binds CD4; IL-2 induces necrosis
Granzymes bind MHC class II; perforin activates complement
Perforin binds CD8; granzymes lyse the CTL

questions.correctOptionText: Perforin forms pores; granzymes induce apoptosis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: perforin permits granzyme entry, and granzymes activate caspases.
distractorRationale.b: Fas ligand binds Fas, and killing is apoptotic.
distractorRationale.c: Neither statement is correct for CTL killing.
distractorRationale.d: Perforin and granzymes act on the target cell, not the CTL.

questions.explanation: CTL granules contain perforin, which makes pores in the target membrane, and granzymes, serine proteases that activate caspases and cause apoptosis. The CTL itself is protected.

questions.stem: Which feature best defines a regulatory T cell?

distractorRationale.b: Correct: Tregs are CD4⁺ CD25⁺ FOXP3⁺.
distractorRationale.d: IgE is an antibody, not a T cell marker.

questions.explanation: Tregs are defined by CD4, high CD25 and FOXP3. They suppress responses via IL-10, TGF-β, IL-2 consumption and CTLA-4.

questions.stem: True or false: CTLs kill target cells by necrosis, causing release of virus particles to neighbouring cells.
questions.explanation: CTLs induce apoptosis through perforin/granzyme and Fas pathways. Apoptosis packages the cell contents, helping to prevent spread of virus, which is why this is the preferred route.

questions.stem: In a release assay the experimental release is 4,200 cpm, spontaneous release is 600 cpm and maximum release is 6,600 cpm. Calculate the percentage specific lysis.
questions.explanation: Specific lysis = (4200 - 600) / (6600 - 600) × 100 = 3600 / 6000 × 100 = 60%. Subtracting spontaneous release corrects for label leaking from intact cells.

questions.stem: Differentiate Th1, Th2 and Th17 cells by driving cytokines, products and the pathogens they target.
markingGuide: Th1: IL-12, T-bet, IFN-γ; intracellular microbes (mycobacteria), macrophage activation
Th2: IL-4, GATA3, IL-4/IL-5/IL-13; helminths, IgE and eosinophils, allergy
Th17: IL-6/TGF-β (IL-23), RORγt, IL-17/IL-22; extracellular bacteria and fungi, neutrophil recruitment
questions.explanation: Each subset arises from distinct cytokine environments and has a tailored effector function.

questions.stem: Describe how a cytotoxic T cell recognises and kills a virus-infected cell.
markingGuide: Recognises viral peptide on MHC class I via TCR with CD8
Perforin forms pores, granzymes enter and activate caspases causing apoptosis
Fas ligand binding Fas as a second pathway
CTL survives and can kill repeatedly; releases IFN-γ and TNF
questions.explanation: The CTL delivers a targeted lethal hit through two apoptotic pathways, sparing neighbouring cells.

questions.stem: Explain how regulatory T cells limit immune responses and what would be expected if FOXP3 function were lost.
markingGuide: Use CTLA-4 to reduce co-stimulation by APCs
Loss of FOXP3 causes widespread autoimmunity (IPEX), enteropathy and endocrine disease in early life
questions.explanation: Tregs are needed to prevent unrestrained effector activity, so their absence causes multi-organ autoimmunity.
